The research on whether video games negatively impact cognitive skills is genuinely mixed and contested. Several high-quality studies report positive cognitive effects: action video games have been associated with improvements in selective attention, sustained attention, task-switching, and visual short-term memory [d1], and experimental training studies have found short-term increases in attentional, visual processing, executive function, and spatial working memory skills from game play [d4]. Active video game play has also been linked to improved decision making and problem solving, suggesting positive effects on some executive functions [d5]. On the other hand, addiction to video games has been firmly linked to worse memory, attention, and cognitive and academic skills in school children [d2], and some sources claim that shooter games may damage the hippocampus, affecting spatial and long-term memory, while producing mixed short-term versus long-term memory outcomes [d6]. Research on violent video games found that their impact on social-cognitive skills is largely limited, with only short-term negative effects observed, and contrary to expectations, habitual exposure was actually related to better inhibitory control in adolescents [d3]. Overall, both positive and negative effects have been documented, with outcomes depending heavily on the type of game, level of addiction, and specific cognitive domain being measured [d1, d2, d5, d7].
